lines.text: רחק 1000 שֹׁבֵב
שׂבב 1000 רתק
נָתַק q. v. in Niph. no. 1.—Frigid is
Cheth. יְרֻחַק to be removed.
Pual רֻתַּק to be bound, Nah. 3, 10.
Deriv. רַתּוֹק and
רְתֻקוֹת f. plur. chains Is. 40, 19.
The letter ש originally, and before the
invention of diacritical signs, served to
express both the simple sound of s, and
also the thicker sound sh. In like man-
ner the Irish language has only one
sign, s, for these two sounds, e. g. solâ
solace, and se (she) he, si (shi) she. At
a later period a distinction was made by
the Grammarians, so that the simple
sound of s came to be indicated by a
point over the left horn, and the thicker
sound sh by one over the right.
For the Heb. שׁ the Chaldee often
and the Syriac always (as being desti-
tute of the letter Sin) substitute ס; see
in lett. ס, p. 707. The Arabic, from a
peculiarity of the language, in almost all
these words has ش; as شنأ שָׂנֵא, שָׂכַר
شكر, שָׂכַל شكل, etc. much as the
people of Wirtemberg give a thicker
sound to the German s, pronouncing ist
like isht. Very rarely does the Arabic
retain س, as שְׂלָו سلوى quail.
In the Hebrew itself, kindred letters
are: a) The other sibilants, as שׂ, ס,
צ, ז, see p. 707; comp. also צָפַן, שָׂפַן,
סָפַן; צָחַק, שָׂחַק; שָׁקַק, זָקַק to strain;
שָׂאַר and שָׁאַר to ferment. b) Some-
times the aspirates, almost like Gr. ὗς
Lat. sus, ὕλη sylva; comp. שָׂדָה i. q. הָדָה
to extend; سلك סָלַךְ i. q. הָלַךְ to go;
שָׂרַג i. q. אָרַג to plait, to weave. Some-
times also, in the formation of roots, a
sibilant is prefixed to the primary bilite-
ral syllable, as שָׂגַב i. q. גָּבַב to be high,
שָׂגָא i. q. גָּאָה, etc. Comp. γράφω scribo,
γλύφω sculpo, τρίζω strideo, tego στέγω,
fallo σφάλλω, and many others.
* שָׁאָה obsol. root, see in שֶׂה.
* רָתַת obsol. root, i. q. רָטַט and Aram.
רְתַת, ܪܰܬ, to terrify; hence
רְתֵת m. terror Hos. 13, 1. Chald.
רְתִיתָא id.
* שָׁאַר obsol. root, kindr. with the
verbs שָׂאַר, סִיר q. v. to become hot, to
ferment; comp. Arab. ثار to boil up, to
break out, as an ulcer. In the western
languages we find from the same stock,
Germ. in Ottfr. suar, Anglosax. sur,
Germ. sauer, Engl. sour.—Hence
Lev. 2, 11. Deut. 16, 4. Chald. סְאֹר id.
שְׂאֵת pr. inf. fem. of the verb נָשָׂא (for
שְׂאֶת), c. suff. שְׂאֵתִי, once contr. שֵׂתוֹ Job
41, 17, where other Mss. have שׂאתו.
1. a lifting up, Job 41, 17 [25]; so of
the countenance, elation, cheerfulness,
Gen. 4, 7. See the root נָשָׂא no. 1. c.
2. elevation, a rising in the skin, hence
14, 56; so too where more than skin
deep, comp. Lev. 13, 2 with v. 3. 4.
3. exaltation, dignity, majesty, Gen.
23. Here too we may refer Hab. 1, 7
from himself go forth his law and his
dignity, i. e. he acknowledges no law
and no dignity but his own.
שָׂב an old man, see in r. שִׂיב.
* שָׂבַךְ to interweave, to braid, i. q.
סָבַךְ. Hence שֹׂבֶךְ, שְׂבָכָה, שׂוֹבֶךְ.
שְׂבָךְ m. only plur. שְׂבָכִים lattices, ba-
lusters, around the capitals of columns,
1 K. 7, 17. See in שְׂבָכָה.
שַׂבְּכָא sambuca, see סַבְּכָא.
שְׂבָכָה f. (r. שָׂבַךְ) 1. a net Job 18, 8.
2. lattice, lattice-work, balustrade, es-
pec. upon or around the capitals of col-
2 Chr. 4, 12. 13. Also before a window
or balcony, 2 K. 1, 2.

line_status.note: Under the nun is a qamets (bar with descending stem), not a hireq dot, and the tav has no dagesh; the dash before "Frigid" is a single em dash, not a doubled one. Reading B matches the print exactly.
The resh carries a single short horizontal stroke (patach), not a qamets with a descending tail, and a dagesh dot is printed inside the tav; this matches the lexicon's form רַתּוֹק "chain".

The printed ש has no shin dot (or any point) above it — consistent with the sense of the passage, which is about the letter before diacritical signs were invented. Reading A's שׁ adds an unprinted dot.

Printed left-to-right after "as" is שָׂנֵא then شنأ (hamza on alif), then ", שָׂכַר"; within that single RTL run the rightmost item شنأ is logically first, so B's order is correct and A's is reversed. Pointing (sin dots, qamets/tsere, qamets/patah) agrees in both.

The only dot above the Hebrew word is the sin dot over ש; there is no holem printed over the final ו, so Reading B's שְׂלָוֹ is wrong. Lamed carries qamets, shin carries sheva, Arabic is سلوى with no points.

Printed left-to-right order after "also" is צָפַן first, then שָׂפַן (Reading A swaps them). The dot on the ש sits on the upper-left arm (sin, as in שָׂחַק on the next line), unlike the right-dotted שׁ in line 1, so שָׂפַן with sin dot is correct.
Printed left-to-right order of the second pair is צָחַק then שָׂחַק (sin dot upper-left), as in Reading B; Reading A swaps them. All points otherwise identical in both readings and match the print.

Decisive point is the left-to-right order: the Arabic سلك is printed first (leftmost), with the Hebrew סָלַךְ to its right, as in Reading A; but the print also has a visible space before both semicolons ("extend ;", "go ;"), as in Reading B. Vowels confirmed: סָלַךְ and הָלַךְ (qamets, patach, final shewa), Arabic unpointed.
Final word is printed שֶׂה: the dot sits on the left arm (sin, as in A) and the vowel below is a three-dot segol (as in B), so A has the wrong vowel and B the wrong shin/sin dot.

Under the resh of both רָתַת and רָטַט the print shows a qamets (horizontal bar with a vertical stroke beneath), not the two stacked dots of sheva; the second letter in each carries a patach. Reading A matches the printed line; B's shevas are wrong.

The Syriac ܪܬ is printed with a vowel sign above the resh — the small wedge/triangle-shaped Western pthaḥa (ܰ) is clearly visible above and between the two letters, distinct from the resh's own intrinsic dot. Reading A omits this point; Reading B includes it. Hebrew רְתַת, punctuation and English agree in both.
The dot over the shin is printed above the right arm (shin dot), not the left (sin dot); Reading A's שָׂ is wrong. Vowels (qamets under shin, patach under aleph) match both readings.

The second Hebrew letter is printed as aleph (א, with its diagonal stroke and two feet), not ayin; it matches the headword שָׂאַר on line 1. Patah under aleph, qamets under shin, סִיר with hireq and yod as both readings have.
The word is printed without vowel points (no tsere, no holam — B is wrong), but a sin dot is visible at the upper left of the shin (A omits it): שׂאתו.

The first derivative after "Hence" is printed defectively (שֹׂבֶךְ, no vav) and the last one plene (שׂוֹבֶךְ, vav clearly visible); Reading A swaps the plene form to first position and gives a non-existent שָׂבָךְ as the third item.

Under the sin of the headword the print shows a shewa (two vertical dots, matching the first item in line 3 "Hence שְׂבָךְ"), not a qamets (A) and not a holem (B); the single dot above is the sin dot only. Rest of the line is as both readings give.
